title: Gratin Dauphinois
subtitle: Potato gratin cooked slowly in cream and garlic
excerpt: Thinly sliced potatoes layered in a garlic-rubbed dish and baked in cream until the potatoes are completely tender and the top is golden and bubbling. One of the most famous potato dishes in France.
sourceNotes: The gratin dauphinois is from the Dauphiné region of south-eastern France, around Grenoble. The earliest known written recipe dates to 1788. The classic version contains no cheese, the gratin forms from the potato starch and cream alone. Elizabeth David, French Provincial Cooking (1960), discusses the cheese question extensively and sides firmly with the no-cheese version. Julia Child, Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961), gives the full method. Gratin dauphinois is distinct from pommes dauphines (fried choux potato balls) and from pommes dauphinoise with cheese, both different dishes.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Gratin dauphinois reheats very well. Cook fully, allow to cool completely, then reheat in a 160°C oven for 25 minutes. The texture actually improves on reheating.

glossaryTerms.definition: A baked dish with a browned, crisp top layer formed by cream, starch, or cheese under oven heat. A gratin dauphinois forms its crust from the potato starch and cream alone, without added cheese.

content.text: The authentic gratin dauphinois, as opposed to the countless versions that add cheese, is one of the most perfectly balanced potato dishes in existence. The cream soaks into the sliced potato as it bakes, the potato starch thickens the cream into a sauce, and the surface gradually browns into a
without any cheese at all. The key is patience: it must bake low and slow for 90 minutes, not 45 minutes at a higher temperature.

items.prepNote: peeled and sliced 3 mm thick, use a mandoline if available
1 halved for rubbing the dish, 1 finely sliced for the gratin

content.text: Heat the oven to 150°C fan. Rub the gratin dish thoroughly with the cut side of the garlic, then butter generously.

Do not wash the sliced potatoes. The starch on the surface is what thickens the cream as the gratin bakes. Layer the potato slices in the dish, overlapping slightly, seasoning each layer generously with salt, pepper, nutmeg, and a few thin slices of garlic.
Mix the cream and milk. Season the mixture. Pour slowly over the potatoes, it should come almost to the top layer but not cover it. The top layer of potato should be just visible above the cream.

Bake uncovered at 150°C fan for 1 hour 30 minutes. The top should be deep golden, the cream should be absorbed and set, and a knife inserted should meet no resistance. If the top browns too fast, cover loosely with foil.
Allow to rest for 10 minutes before serving. Serve from the dish.

items.symptom: The cream has curdled in the oven
items.cause: The oven temperature was too high, or the cream quality was poor.
items.fix: Keep the temperature at or below 150°C fan. A rolling boil causes cream to split; the low temperature ensures it barely simmers throughout. The potato starch helps stabilise the cream as it heats.

items.symptom: The potatoes are still firm after 90 minutes
items.cause: The slices were too thick, or the oven runs cool.
items.fix: Slice potatoes at 3 mm maximum, use a mandoline for consistency. If they are still firm after 90 minutes, continue at 160°C for a further 20 to 30 minutes.

items.symptom: The gratin is soggy rather than creamy
items.cause: The potatoes were washed after slicing, removing the starch that thickens the cream.
items.fix: Do not wash the sliced potatoes. The starch is essential to the final texture.

content.text: The Dauphiné is the pre-Alpine region centred on Grenoble, in the south-east of France. The gratin dauphinois appears in the municipal records of Grenoble in 1788, where it was served at a banquet for the city's military governor. The dish's spread across France was gradual but irresistible; it is now the most copied of all French potato dishes. The cheese version (often called gratin dauphinoise or pommes dauphinoise) is a widespread adaptation, but the purists of Grenoble maintain that the original never contained it.
